questions.stem: A user with Windows Home tries to join the company Active Directory domain but the option is unavailable. What is the cause?

choices.text: The domain controller is unreachable
Windows Home cannot join an Active Directory domain
The user lacks local admin rights
The workgroup name conflicts with the domain name

questions.explanation: Windows Home does not support Active Directory domain join. The option is grayed out. The machine must be upgraded to Pro or higher.
questions.trap: The other options are possible in theory but the scenario says the option is unavailable - that is the Home edition limitation.

questions.stem: A share named 'Payroll$' is created on a file server. A contractor knows the server name. What is TRUE about this share?

choices.text: The contractor cannot connect because $ shares require domain credentials
The share is invisible in Network browse lists but accessible via direct UNC path if permissions allow
The $ suffix encrypts the share contents in transit
The share is completely hidden from all users including administrators

questions.explanation: A $ share is only hidden from the browse list. Anyone who knows the UNC path (\\server\Payroll$) can attempt to connect - permissions control whether they succeed.
questions.trap: Hiding does not equal securing. Use NTFS/share permissions for actual access control.

questions.stem: A technician needs to map a network drive to the share \\filesvr\Reports using the command line. Which command is correct?

choices.text: net share R: \\filesvr\Reports
net use R: \\filesvr\Reports
map R: \\filesvr\Reports
netsh add drive R: \\filesvr\Reports

questions.explanation: net use maps a drive letter to a UNC share path. net share is for creating shares on the local machine, not mapping remote ones.
questions.trap: net share vs net use: 'share' exposes local resources, 'use' connects to remote ones.

questions.stem: A Windows 11 firewall rule must block all unencrypted HTTP traffic arriving on TCP port 80. Which firewall component and action should the technician use?

choices.text: Outbound rule, action: Block, protocol: TCP, port: 80
Inbound rule, action: Block, protocol: TCP, port: 80
Connection security rule, action: Block, protocol: TCP, port: 80
Inbound rule, action: Allow if secure, protocol: UDP, port: 80

questions.explanation: Blocking unsolicited inbound HTTP requires an inbound rule, TCP protocol, port 80, action Block. Outbound rules control traffic leaving the machine.
questions.trap: Connection security rules configure IPsec, not simple port blocking.

questions.stem: A workstation running ipconfig shows an IP of 169.254.43.22. What is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: A static IP was manually configured in this range
The DHCP server is unreachable and the device self-assigned an APIPA address
The device is using IPv6 link-local addressing
The DNS server failed to respond

questions.explanation: 169.254.x.x is the APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) range, assigned automatically when DHCP is unavailable. The technician should investigate the DHCP server and network connectivity.
questions.trap: (c) IPv6 link-local is fe80::/10, not 169.254.x.x. DNS failure does not affect the IP address assignment.

questions.stem: A technician pings 127.0.0.1 successfully but cannot reach the default gateway. What does the successful loopback ping confirm?

choices.text: The local network cable is functional
The local TCP/IP stack is initialised and working
DNS resolution is working correctly
The default gateway is reachable via IPv6

questions.explanation: Loopback (127.0.0.1) tests the local TCP/IP stack only - no traffic leaves the NIC. A successful result rules out a broken IP stack.
questions.trap: Loopback says nothing about the physical link, DNS, or the gateway - those require additional tests.

questions.stem: A company deploys new WPA2 wireless access points. The security team asks which encryption cipher to configure. What is correct?

choices.text: TKIP, because it is the default for WPA2
AES, because WPA2 requires AES
WEP, because it is backward compatible with WPA2 hardware
TKIP/AES mixed mode to support both old and new clients

questions.explanation: WPA2 uses AES (CCMP) as its encryption cipher. TKIP is the legacy cipher from WPA1 and should not be used on WPA2 deployments.
questions.trap: TKIP is the classic wrong answer for WPA2. Mixed mode appears on some APs but the exam answer is AES for WPA2/WPA3.

questions.stem: A laptop user connects to a hotel Wi-Fi. Windows asks whether the network is public or private. What should the user select and why?

choices.text: Private - so file sharing works with other hotel guests
Public - to disable inbound connections and file sharing on an untrusted network
Domain - because the hotel may have a central authentication server
Private - because public profile blocks Windows Update

questions.explanation: Public profile disables file sharing and blocks unsolicited inbound connections - the correct choice for any untrusted network. Private is for known, trusted networks only.
questions.trap: Domain profile only appears when the device is joined to an AD domain. Public does not block Windows Update.

questions.stem: A remote worker tethers their phone as a hotspot to connect a laptop. Background app updates are consuming mobile data. What Windows setting limits this?

choices.text: Set the network profile to Public
Enable metered connection for the hotspot adapter
Disable Windows Update via Group Policy
Turn off the Windows Defender Firewall for the private profile

questions.explanation: Marking the connection as metered tells Windows to reduce background data: it throttles Windows Update, OneDrive sync, and app updates. The setting is per adapter in Settings > Network and Internet.
questions.trap: Disabling Group Policy or the firewall is destructive and does not address background bandwidth consumption.

questions.stem: Order the steps of the Windows Defender Firewall New Rule wizard (Advanced Security) from first to last.

items.text: Select rule type: Program, Port, Predefined, or Custom
Specify local and remote IP scope
Choose action: Allow, Allow if secure, or Block
Select which profiles the rule applies to (Domain / Private / Public)
Enter a name and optional description

questions.explanation: The wizard proceeds: type > protocol/port > IP scope > action > profiles > name. Knowing this order helps eliminate wrong answers on scenario questions.

questions.stem: Match each networking scenario to the correct Windows feature.

pairs.rightText: Hidden share - $ suffix on share name

pairs.leftText: Laptop roams between DHCP and fixed-IP network
Throttle Windows Update on cellular hotspot
Encrypt VPN tunnel to corporate office

questions.explanation: These are the five most-tested networking features on the 220-1202 exam.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about Windows network profiles are TRUE? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The Domain profile appears only when the device is joined to an Active Directory domain
Public profile disables file sharing and blocks inbound connections
Private profile is the safest choice for coffee shop networks
Windows prompts you to choose a profile when first connecting to a new network

questions.explanation: (c) is false - Public is the correct choice for untrusted networks. Private is for home or work networks where you trust other devices.
questions.trap: Choosing Private for an unknown network is the classic mistake. Public = untrusted, Private = trusted.
